parts:

I am estimating a version of a dynamic ecological inference model. The model allows future information on interior cell proportions to inform estimates for other periods when only the marginal proportions are observed. It does so with a Dirichlet transition model for the cell proportions, as in:
props[t] ~ dirichlet(props[t - 1] * priorN);
I use a uniform prior for the proportions in t=1.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Problem with multimodality (Dirichlet parameters in one chain stuck near 0)
parts:
This is not multimodality but rather a failure of convergence.  In particular, you should be seeing n_divergent=1
for many, if not most, iterations.  The problem is the extreme curvature near zero which causes the gradients,
and hence the HMC transitions, to fail.

An immediate option is to decrease the step size (or increase the target average acceptance probability in the
adaptation).  Alternatively you can try to find a parameterization that reduces the change in curvature.  Lastly
you can reduce the curvature by smoothing out your model, as you have done.

parts:
Just declare props as a simplex type, which will implicitly apply the best transforms.

In CmdStan just set adapt delta=0.9 (or 0.95, 0.99, increasing until n_divergence is always zero).  The other defaults will change (or not) as necessary automatically.  In general increasing the target average acceptance probability may lead to smaller efficiency but it will always lead to a more robust sampler so it’s a very safe knob to turn.

parts: To follow up again: I tried setting adapt_delta to .9, .95, and .99, and it didn't seem to affect the output.

Did the final step size drop?  The dependence of the final step size on the target average acceptance probability is highly nonlinear so you may have to turn adaptation off and set the step size yourself.
One or two chains would always get stuck somewhere far from the others. Also, the problem doesn't seem to have much to do with n_divergent.

Yes, it does. Basically n_divergent != 0 indicates that there is a pathological region of phase space and with some probability any chain will eventually get stuck (or run long enough and the probability that it will get stuck at least once goes to unity).  It’s not the proportion of 1s, it’s whether you see any at all (technically, the proportion is more related to how big the pathological region is).

If you ran and saw a nontrivial number of divergent iterations but none of the chains got stuck that doesn’t mean the results are valid — you just lucked out and didn’t get stuck.  The expectations are still biased.

In every chain, n_divergent=1 in 2–5% of iterations, and the proportion of 1s appeared to be unrelated to getting stuck. Specifying a more informative prior is more effective at avoiding the problem but isn't fool-proof. Also, I should clarify that I was already declaring props as a simplex, and that I am using rstan Version 2.4.0.

More informative priors soften the curvature changes around the boundary and you should see the proportion of n_divergent iterations drop correspondingly.  Typically these kinds of problems arise in hierarchical models and we get around them with non-centered parameterizations, but without seeing your model it’s not clear if there would be an equivalent reparameterization.

`  # Get sampler parameters

      lapply(sampler_params, FUN = function(x) {step <- table(x[,"stepsize__"]); names(step)[step == max(step)]})

      lapply(sampler_params, FUN = function(x) mean(x[,"accept_stat__"]))

parts: > Thanks again for the clarification, Michael. As you can tell, I have many things to learn about how Stan actually works on the inside.
We’re learning, too. A lot of the practical advice is coming from the latest things we’ve learned about HMC heoretically and much of it is relatively novel for typical MCMC algorithms.
> Your response makes me think that if I can't completely eliminate the n_divergent = 1 problem, maybe the best solution is simply to run multiple chains and throw out the ones that get stuck.

This is what you absolutely don’t want to do.

Let’s assume that the pathological region is around a boundary at zero. What the divergences are telling you is that there is a small region near zero with significant probability mass that will effect all of your Monte Carlo estimates, but the step size of the sampler is too large for HMC to be able to explore that region. Most of the time the region just gets ignored, and occasionally the sampler will be in just the right position to jump into the region but then it cannot escape. In either case the resulting expectations will be biased so none of the chains will be valid.

Unless all of your chains report n_divergent=0 we cannot guarantee the accuracy of your Monte Carlo estimates.

Incidentally, this kind of pathology occurs in Random Walk Metropolis and the Gibbs sampler, too, only there’s rarely an indication that something is going wrong (no n_divergent equivalent). At least HMC is informing us that something is afoul!
> By the way, I don't know how to check the final step size, so I don't know whether increasing adapt_delta to 0.99 succeeded in decreasing it.
The step size should be output in the summary call.  I’m not an RStan user myself so I won’t be of much help here.

parts:
Step size is just a single value, but then there's also
a mass matrix that's estimated from the warmup sample covariance.
The default is a diagonal mass matrix with varying entries, but
you can insist on a unit matrix (forcing a single step size everywhere)
or use a dense mass matrix.

Numerical algorithms often run into problems when you get this kind
of poor conditioning --- matrix inversions with high ratios of highest
to lowest eigenvalue or stiff diff eq solvers (different dimensions evolving
at different time scales). But Stan should be able to handle scales that
vary in dimension.

A bigger problem is usually that if you have something like a hierarchical
model, where the scale changes with the hierarchical parameter.

- Bob

parts:
Hey, sorry, I missed the replay with the metric components.

As Bob notes scales are set in two ways. We estimate the marginal
variance of each parameter to set the diagonal element of the metric
(diagonal by default in Stan) and then we have an overall scaling
set by the step size of the integrator.

Now one immediate problem is the absolute size of your metric
components. 1e-6 is a tiny marginal variance, and may be running
into problems with our own adaptation algorithm which uses a
prior on the marginal variances of the order 1e-6 (that shrinks
with more warmup samples). So some of those marginal
variances may be too big which is forces the step size to be
small to compensate and causing poor performance all around.

Marginal variances that small could also be an indication of really
large autocorrelations and way too little warmup. In any case it
seems like the model may be too complex (folk theorem, etc).
Do you have hierarchical structure? Are you using a non-centered
parameterization?

Another thing to look at is wether or not you’re saturating the
maximum three depth. If so then NUTS is terminating early and
you’re not fully leveraging the power of HMC. Saturation
is indicative of model problems and increasing the max depth
would only be a weak bandaid, but it may help.

When models start misbehaving this badly we can only speculate
without actually seeing code, unfortunately.

data {

  simplex[N] props0;
  int<lower=0> countsT1M1[96];
  matrix<lower=0,upper=1>[96, N] iotaT1M1;
  int<lower=0> countsT1M2[2];
  matrix<lower=0,upper=1>[2, N] iotaT1M2;
  int<lower=0> countsT2M1[2];
  matrix<lower=0,upper=1>[2, N] iotaT2M1;
  int<lower=0> countsT3M1[4];
  matrix<lower=0,upper=1>[4, N] iotaT3M1;
  int<lower=0> countsT4M1[96];
  matrix<lower=0,upper=1>[96, N] iotaT4M1;
  int<lower=0> countsT4M2[4];
  matrix<lower=0,upper=1>[4, N] iotaT4M2;
  int<lower=0> countsT5M1[4];
  matrix<lower=0,upper=1>[4, N] iotaT5M1;
  int<lower=0> countsT6M1[96];
  matrix<lower=0,upper=1>[96, N] iotaT6M1;
  int<lower=0> countsT7M1[192];
  matrix<lower=0,upper=1>[192, N] iotaT7M1;
}
parameters {
  simplex[N] props[T]; // period-specific cell probabilities
}
model {
for (t in 1:T) {

if (t == 1) {
      props[t] ~ dirichlet(props0 * priorN);
    }
    if (t > 1) {
      props[t] ~ dirichlet(props[t - 1] * transitN / Tgaps[t]);
    }
  }
  countsT1M1 ~ multinomial(iotaT1M1 * props[1]);
  countsT1M2 ~ multinomial(iotaT1M2 * props[1]);
  countsT2M1 ~ multinomial(iotaT2M1 * props[2]);

  countsT6M1 ~ multinomial(iotaT6M1 * props[6]);
  countsT7M1 ~ multinomial(iotaT7M1 * props[7]);
}

Devin

Why are you multiplying the multinomial parameters? props[n] should already
be a simplex, and the multinomial does validate that its argument is a simplex,
so multiplying by anything other than 1 should produce an error.

I'd also suggest simplifying this:

for (t in 1:T) {
if (t == 1) {
props[t] ~ dirichlet(props0 * priorN);
}
if (t > 1) {
props[t] ~ dirichlet(props[t - 1] * transitN / Tgaps[t]);
}
}

to

props[1] ~ dirichlet(props0 * priorN);
for (t in 2:T)
props[t] ~ dirichlet(props[t - 1] * transitN / Tgaps[t]);

Too bad we don't have a vectorized version of multinomial yet, because
it'd really simplify the multinomial sampling in your program.

- Bob

Hi Bob,

Thanks for the simplification suggestion. With regard to multiplying the multinomial parameters, let me clarify. Each element of "props" is a vector of proportions corresponding to the cells created by a cross-tabulation of multiple demographic categories (e.g., FEMALE by BLACK by SOUTHERN). In most periods, the cell-specific counts are not observed. Instead, we observe marginal counts (e.g., countsT1M1) in lower-dimensional cross-classifications (e.g., FEMALE by BLACK). To sum the cell proportions into the coarser categories, the code premultiplies the props vector by an indicator matrix (e.g., iotaT1M1 * props[1]). This results in another simplex of proportions the same length as the count vector.

It occurs to me that maybe it would be better to first define the vector of multinomial parameters as a separate parameter (also a simplex), as in: 
simplex[96] propsT1M1;
propsT1M1 <- iotaT1M1 * props[1]
countsT1M1 ~ multinomial(propsT1M1)
Would that help Stan handle the model better?

Sorry for not providing more information on the model earlier. I was trying to avoid overloading you with details.

Thanks for your help,
Devin

Why are you multiplying the multinomial parameters?  props[n] should already
be a simplex, and the multinomial does validate that its argument is a simplex,
so multiplying by anything other than 1 should produce an error.

I'd also suggest simplifying this:

  for (t in 1:T) {
    if (t == 1) {

    if (t > 1) {

to

  props[1] ~ dirichlet(props0 * priorN);
  for (t in 2:T)
    props[t] ~ dirichlet(props[t - 1] * transitN / Tgaps[t]);

Too bad we don't have a vectorized version of multinomial yet, because
it'd really simplify the multinomial sampling in your program.

- Bob
